Empirical Research Plan: “How Do Incumbents Respond to the Threat of Southwest Entry?”

------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) combined with an event-study panel.

Rationale
• The “treatment’’—Southwest becoming operational at both endpoint airports of a city-pair—creates a large, plausibly exogenous jump in the probability of future entry on that specific route, while nothing changes immediately for consumers (no Southwest flights yet).  
• Treatment timing varies by route, producing quasi-experimental, staggered adoption.  
• We observe the same routes before and after treatment and can compare them to routes that have not (yet) become “threatened.”  
• An event study lets us trace incumbents’ pricing/capacity responses relative to treatment quarter τ = 0 and verify pre-trends.  
• All key outcomes (fares, seats, flights, passengers) are observed at quarterly frequency over 12 years, satisfying DID data requirements.

Why not IV/RDD?
– There is no obvious continuous running variable with a known cutoff (RDD).  
– A two-stage IV (e.g., instrumenting actual entry with threat) would answer a different question.  
DID directly measures the incumbent response to the threat itself, which is the target.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment definition (binary T_rt):
T_rt = 1 if, in quarter t, Southwest is already serving both endpoint airports of route r, BUT is not yet flying that route.

Control group:
Routes r’ in the same airport-pair sample and period t that have not yet reached the “both-endpoints’’ condition.

Sample restrictions
• Drop route-quarters after Southwest’s first actual flight on the route (to cleanly separate “threat’’ from “entry’’ effects).  
• Keep all incumbent carriers (American, Continental, Delta, Northwest, TWA, United, US Airways) that ever served the route in the window −8 ≤ τ ≤ +8 quarters around treatment.

Treatment timing / event date:
Quarter τ = 0 is the first quarter in which Southwest simultaneously serves both endpoints.

Notation:
y_i,r,t — outcome for incumbent i on route r at quarter t  
τ_r,t — event time (t – treatment quarter_r)  
γ_r — route fixed effects  
δ_t — calendar-quarter*year fixed effects to absorb industry-wide shocks

Main DID specification:
y_i,r,t = β · Threat_r,t + γ_r + δ_t + X_i,r,tθ + ε_i,r,t

Event study (leads/lags):
y_i,r,t = Σ_{k≠−1} β_k · 1{τ=k} + γ_r + δ_t + X_i,r,tθ + ε_i,r,t  
(normalize k = −1, the quarter before treatment)

------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: Absent the threat, treated and control routes would have evolved similarly in fares/capacity.  
Plausibility: Incumbents mainly set prices route-by-route; quarterly dummies, route FE, and common demand shifters (GDP, fuel, 9/11, SARS) are absorbed. Pre-trend tests in event study will be implemented.

A2. No simultaneous confounding shocks correlated with treatment timing.  
Plausibility: Southwest’s decision to fly both endpoints is driven mostly by airport agreements and its city-presence strategy, unlikely to be tightly linked to incumbents’ route-specific demand shocks.

A3. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA): Treatment on one route does not spill over to control routes (or the spillovers are minimal).  
Plausibility: Possible network pricing interactions exist, but we can cluster s.e.’s by airport pair and test for spillovers on geographically adjacent routes as robustness.

A4. Composition stability: Entry and exit of incumbent carriers on the route are not driven by the threat itself in the pre-period.  
Plausibility: Large carriers rarely abandon profitable routes merely because Southwest gains airport presence; we can verify by showing the number of incumbent carriers is stable pre-threat.

------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Endogenous Southwest airport expansion.  
   – Remedy: Control for airport*quarter shocks (two-way fixed effects at each endpoint), or interact airport FE with linear time trends.  
   – Placebo: Apply the same treatment definition to a “pseudo-Southwest’’ (e.g., JetBlue) and verify no pre-treatment effects.

T2. Anticipatory incumbent behavior before τ = −1 (i.e., when lease negotiations become public).  
   – Remedy: Extend event-study window to τ = −8. If β_{k<0} ≠ 0 well before τ=0, redefine treatment to earlier “announcement’’ quarter using Lexis-Nexis dates and rerun.

T3. Post-treatment contamination by actual entry within a few quarters.  
   – Remedy: Censor the sample at τ = +Q where Q is the quarter before Southwest’s first flight; baseline Q=3. Re-estimate with alternative Q (2,4,6).

------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
------------------------------------------------------------
```r
#----------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Libraries
#----------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)     # fast manipulation
library(fixest)         # high-dimensional FE
library(ggplot2)

#----------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load and merge DB1A and T100
#----------------------------------------------------------
db1a  <- fread("db1a_route_carrier_qtr.csv")   # fares & pax
t100  <- fread("t100_route_carrier_qtr.csv")   # seats & flights
threat<- fread("threat_dates.csv")             # endpoint_presence & actual_entry

# Merge
panel <- merge(db1a, t100, 
               by = c("route", "carrier", "quarter"), all.x = TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, threat, by = "route", all.x = TRUE)

#----------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Construct variables
#----------------------------------------------------------
panel[, treated := 0L]
panel[quarter >= both_endpoints_qtr & quarter < sw_entry_qtr, 
      treated := 1L]

# Event-time
panel[, event_time := quarter - both_endpoints_qtr]

# Trim symmetric window −8:+8 around treatment
panel <- panel[event_time >= -8 & event_time <= 8]

# Outcomes
panel[, ln_fare := log(avg_fare)]
panel[, ln_pax  := log(passengers + 1)]
panel[, ln_seats:= log(seats + 1)]
panel[, ln_flights:= log(flights + 1)]

#----------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main DID
#----------------------------------------------------------
did_fit <- feols(ln_fare ~ treated | route + quarter, 
                 data = panel, cluster = ~route)
summary(did_fit)

#----------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Event study (leave out k = −1)
#----------------------------------------------------------
for_ES <- panel[ event_time != -1 ]
for_ES[, f_event := factor(event_time)]
es_fit <- feols(ln_fare ~ i(event_time, ref = -1) | route + quarter, 
                data = for_ES, cluster = ~route)
etable(es_fit, se.below = TRUE)

# Plot coefficients
es_coef <- data.frame(
  k  = as.numeric(names(es_fit$coefficients)),
  beta = es_fit$coefficients,
  se   = es_fit$se
)
ggplot(es_coef, aes(x = k, y = beta)) +
  geom_point() + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = beta - 1.96*se, ymax = beta + 1.96*se)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
  theme_minimal() + labs(x = "Quarters relative to threat", y = "Δ ln fare")

#----------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness: censor obs <=2 quarters before actual entry
#----------------------------------------------------------
panel_rb <- panel[ quarter < sw_entry_qtr - 2 ]
did_rb <- feols(ln_fare ~ treated | route + quarter, 
                data = panel_rb, cluster = ~route)
summary(did_rb)
```

------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
------------------------------------------------------------
Economic intuition (contestable market theory + pricing to deter entry) suggests:

• Fares: Incumbents will cut fares preemptively to raise potential entrant’s hurdle. Magnitude: roughly 5-10 percent (−0.05 to −0.10 in logs), larger on high-density “must-have’’ routes.  
• Capacity: Two plausible strategic responses  
   – Accommodation view: increase seats to lock in loyalty (≈ +5%).  
   – Deterrence view: temporarily flood capacity (+10–15%). My prior leans toward a modest capacity expansion (+5–8%).  

I therefore expect β̂_fare ≈ −0.07 and β̂_seats ≈ +0.06.

------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Parallel pre-trends visually confirmed ....................................... 1  
C2. No differential time-varying shocks (airport*quarter FE) ..................... 0.8  
C3. No spillovers to control units ............................................... 0.7  
C4. Stable composition of incumbents ............................................ 0.9  
C5. Correct standard-error clustering (route-level) .............................. 1  
Overall DID validity score ≈ 4.4/5

------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
